title: Entropy
html:
Guiding question

What determines the direction of chemical change?

The whole of R1.4 is Additional Higher Level. Enthalpy alone cannot tell us whether a reaction will happen: some endothermic processes (dissolving NH4NO3, melting ice above 0 °C, the Ba(OH)2 + NH4SCN demonstration) happen on their own. To predict the direction of change we also need entropy, and the two are combined in the Gibbs energy, ΔG.

R1.4.1 Entropy AHL

DefinitionEntropy, S, is a measure of the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system. The more ways the particles and their energy can be arranged, the higher the entropy. It is often described as the "disorder" of a system.

Think about the class starter: what happens to the particles as a solid melts? They gain energy, break free of their fixed positions and can move past each other, so there are many more ways to arrange them and their energy. "Everything in the universe is, over time, moving to greater disorder": a log fire turning solid fuel into ash and gas, or ice cubes melting in a drink, are everyday examples.

Entropy has units of J K−1 mol−1 (note: joules, not kilojoules). Standard entropy, S⦵, is the entropy of one mole of a substance at 100 kPa and 298 K; values are in the data booklet. Unlike ΔHf, the S⦵ of an element is not zero, and all S⦵ values are positive (a perfect crystal has zero entropy only at 0 K).

What gives a substance higher entropy?

  • State: S(solid) < S(liquid) < S(gas). Gas particles move freely and randomly and can be arranged in far more ways. For water, S⦵(H2O, l) = 70 and S⦵(H2O, g) = 189 J K−1 mol−1.
  • Temperature: heating a substance increases entropy, because the particles have more energy and there are more ways to distribute it.
  • Complexity: molecules with more atoms have more ways to vibrate and rotate, so higher entropy: S⦵(NO2) = 240 > S⦵(NO) = 211 J K−1 mol−1; CO2 > CO.
  • Mixing and dissolving: a solution has higher entropy than the separate pure solute and solvent; NaCl(aq) > NaCl(s).
  • Number of particles: more moles (especially of gas) means more possible arrangements.

On a graph of entropy against temperature, S rises gradually as a solid, liquid or gas is heated, with sudden vertical jumps at the melting point and the boiling point. The jump at boiling is much larger than at melting, because the change from liquid to gas produces a far bigger increase in freedom of movement.

Which has the higher entropy in each pair? (i) NaCl(aq) or NaCl(s); (ii) CO or CO2; (iii) H2O at 25 °C or at 50 °C

  1. NaCl(s), CO, 25 °C
  2. NaCl(aq), CO2, 50 °C
  3. NaCl(aq), CO, 50 °C
  4. NaCl(s), CO2, 25 °C

A solution is more dispersed than a solid; CO2 has more atoms, so more ways to vibrate and rotate; higher temperature means more energy to distribute.

The standard entropy of H2O(g) is 189 J K−1 mol−1. Which value is most likely for H2O(l)?

  1. 70
  2. 189
  3. 450
  4. 699

The liquid has much lower entropy than the gas: 70 J K−1 mol−1 (data booklet). Values like 699 would be impossible for such a small molecule.

title: Predicting and calculating ΔS
html:
Predicting the sign of ΔS AHL

Key pointLook first at the number of moles of gas. If it increases, ΔS is positive; if it decreases, ΔS is negative. If the moles of gas stay the same, look at changes in state (solid → liquid/aqueous increases S) or say that the change is too small to predict.
ReactionSign of ΔSReason
CH3OH(l) → CH3OH(g)+liquid → gas
N2O4(g) → 2NO2(g)+1 → 2 mol gas
2KClO3(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g)+gas formed from solid
CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)+gas formed
Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)+gas formed
2NH3(g) + H2SO4(aq) → (NH4)2SO4(aq)−2 mol gas used up
Ba2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)−aqueous ions → solid (precipitation)
2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g)−3 → 2 mol gas
MgO(s) + CO2(g) → MgCO3(s)−gas used up
2N2(g) + O2(g) → 2N2O(g)−3 → 2 mol gas
PCl5(s) → PCl3(l) + Cl2(g)+gas formed from solid
N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g)≈ 02 → 2 mol gas; too close to call by inspection

Which reactions have a positive entropy change? I 2N2(g) + O2(g) → 2N2O(g); II CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g); III Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

I goes from 3 mol of gas to 2 mol of gas, so ΔS is negative (not "too close to tell"). II and III both produce a gas from non-gaseous reactants.

Which reactions have a negative entropy change? I 2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g); II MgO(s) + CO2(g) → MgCO3(s); III PCl5(s) → PCl3(l) + Cl2(g)

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

I: 3 → 2 mol gas. II: gas used up. III makes a gas from a solid, so its ΔS is positive.

Increase, decrease or too close to tell? H2O(l) → H2O(g); NaCl(s) → Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq); H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g); Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s); 2N2O5(g) → 4NO2(g) + O2(g); H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l)

Increase (liquid → gas); increase (solid → aqueous ions); about the same (2 → 2 mol gas); decrease (precipitation); increase (2 → 5 mol gas); decrease (two aqueous ions → one liquid molecule).

Calculating ΔS⦵ AHL

ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants)

Multiply each S⦵ by its coefficient in the equation, and remember elements have non-zero values. The layout is the same as for ΔH from ΔHf data.

Worked example

Calculate ΔS⦵ for N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). S⦵ / J K−1 mol−1: N2 192, H2 131, NH3 193.

ΔS⦵ = 2(193) − [192 + 3(131)] = 386 − 585 = −199 J K−1 mol−1.

Sense check: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so a negative value is expected.

Calculate ΔS⦵ for H2O(g) → H2O(l). S⦵: H2O(g) 189, H2O(l) 70 J K−1 mol−1.

ΔS⦵ = 70 − 189 = −119 J K−1 mol−1. Negative: condensing makes the system more ordered.

Calculate ΔS⦵ for C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(l). S⦵: C3H8 270, O2 205, CO2 214, H2O(l) 70 J K−1 mol−1.

Products: 3(214) + 4(70) = 642 + 280 = 922. Reactants: 270 + 5(205) = 1295. ΔS⦵ = 922 − 1295 = −373 J K−1 mol−1 (6 mol gas → 3 mol gas plus a liquid).

Calculate the standard entropy change of formation of copper(I) oxide: 2Cu(s) + ½O2(g) → Cu2O(s). S⦵: Cu 33.3, O2 205, Cu2O 101 J K−1 mol−1.

Reactants: 2(33.3) + ½(205) = 66.6 + 102.5 = 169.1. ΔS⦵ = 101 − 169.1 = −68.1 J K−1 mol−1. Elements do not have zero entropy.

title: Total entropy and the second law
html:
Entropy of the surroundings and total entropy AHL

The second law of thermodynamics says that in a spontaneous change the total entropy of the universe increases. An exothermic reaction releases heat into the surroundings, which increases the entropy of the surroundings. That is why many exothermic reactions are spontaneous even when ΔSsystem is negative.

ΔSsurroundings = −ΔHsystem ÷ T     ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings

A process is spontaneous when ΔStotal > 0. Convert ΔH from kJ to J before dividing by T.

Worked example

Does NaBr dissolve spontaneously at 298 K? NaBr(s) → Na+(aq) + Br−(aq), ΔH⦵ = −0.6 kJ mol−1, ΔS⦵system = +55.0 J K−1 mol−1.

ΔSsurroundings = −(−600 J) ÷ 298 K = +2.0 J K−1 mol−1.

ΔStotal = 55.0 + 2.0 = +57.0 J K−1 mol−1; positive, so dissolving is spontaneous.

Multiplying ΔStotal by −T gives −TΔStotal = ΔH − TΔSsystem, which is the Gibbs energy change. So "ΔStotal positive" and "ΔG negative" are the same condition.

Worked example

Burning calcium. 2Ca(s) + O2(g) → 2CaO(s), ΔH⦵ = −1270 kJ (for 2 mol CaO). S⦵: Ca 41.6, O2 205, CaO 40 J K−1 mol−1.

  1. ΔSsystem = 2(40) − [2(41.6) + 205] = 80 − 288.2 = −208.2 J K−1.
  2. ΔSsurroundings = −(−1 270 000 J) ÷ 298 K = +4261.7 J K−1.
  3. ΔStotal = −208.2 + 4261.7 = +4053.5 J K−1.

The system becomes more ordered (a gas is used up), but the huge amount of heat released spreads energy into the surroundings, so the total entropy increases and the reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous.

A process has ΔH = −50.0 kJ mol−1 and ΔSsystem = −120 J K−1 mol−1. Calculate ΔStotal at 298 K.

ΔSsurroundings = −(−50 000) ÷ 298 = +167.8 J K−1 mol−1. ΔStotal = −120 + 167.8 = +47.8 J K−1 mol−1: spontaneous at 298 K.

Why are many exothermic reactions spontaneous even when the entropy of the system decreases?

  1. Exothermic reactions always have positive ΔSsystem
  2. The heat released increases the entropy of the surroundings by more than the system loses
  3. Heat released lowers the temperature of the surroundings
  4. ΔS does not matter for exothermic reactions

ΔSsurroundings = −ΔH/T is positive for an exothermic reaction, and at moderate temperatures it can outweigh a negative ΔSsystem.

Predict first: water freezes, H2O(l) → H2O(s), ΔH = −6.01 kJ mol−1, ΔSsystem = −22.0 J K−1 mol−1. Is freezing spontaneous at 263 K (−10 °C) and at 283 K (+10 °C)? Reveal to check

At 263 K: ΔSsurr = 6010 ÷ 263 = +22.9; ΔStotal = −22.0 + 22.9 = +0.9 J K−1 mol−1, so water freezes. At 283 K: ΔSsurr = 6010 ÷ 283 = +21.2; ΔStotal = −0.8, so it does not; ice melts instead. The changeover is at 6010 ÷ 22.0 = 273 K, the melting point. Temperature controls how much the heat released matters to the surroundings.

title: Gibbs energy and spontaneity
html:
R1.4.2 Spontaneity and Gibbs energy AHL

DefinitionA spontaneous (thermodynamically feasible) reaction is one that, once started, proceeds without a continuous input of energy from outside. It does not have to go to completion, and it says nothing about how fast it goes. A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is negative. When ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium; when ΔG is positive the reaction is not spontaneous in the forward direction (the reverse reaction is spontaneous).
ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵    (data booklet, section 1)
Common mistakeUnits. ΔH is in kJ mol−1 but ΔS is in J K−1 mol−1. Divide ΔS by 1000 (or multiply ΔH by 1000) before substituting. T must be in kelvin (°C + 273). Most lost marks on Gibbs questions come from these two slips.

ΔGf⦵ values. ΔG can also be found from standard Gibbs energies of formation, just like ΔH: ΔG⦵ = ΣΔGf⦵(products) − ΣΔGf⦵(reactants). ΔGf⦵ of an element in its standard state is zero. Values calculated this way are valid only at 298 K.

Worked example

Calculate ΔG⦵ at 298 K for 2Fe(s) + 1½O2(g) → Fe2O3(s). ΔH⦵ = −822 kJ mol−1. S⦵ / J K−1 mol−1: Fe 27.2, O2 205, Fe2O3 90.0.

  1. ΔS⦵ = 90.0 − [2(27.2) + 1.5(205)] = 90.0 − 361.9 = −271.9 J K−1 mol−1 = −0.2719 kJ K−1 mol−1.
  2. ΔG⦵ = −822 − 298(−0.2719) = −822 + 81.0 = −741 kJ mol−1.

ΔG is very negative, so rusting is thermodynamically spontaneous. Yet iron rusts slowly: ΔG says nothing about the rate, which depends on the activation energy (kinetics, R2.2).

Key pointSpontaneous does not mean fast. Diamond turning into graphite has a negative ΔG at room temperature, but the rate is so slow that it never happens on a human timescale. A negative ΔG tells you a reaction can happen, not that it will happen quickly.

CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). ΔHf: CaCO3 −1207, CaO −635, CO2 −394 kJ mol−1; S⦵: CaCO3 93, CaO 40, CO2 214 J K−1 mol−1. Calculate ΔG⦵ at 298 K.

ΔH = (−635 − 394) − (−1207) = +178 kJ mol−1. ΔS = (40 + 214) − 93 = +161 J K−1 mol−1 = 0.161 kJ K−1 mol−1.
ΔG = 178 − 298(0.161) = +130 kJ mol−1. Positive, so limestone does not decompose at room temperature.

NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s). ΔHf: NH3 −46, HCl −95, NH4Cl −315 kJ mol−1; S⦵: NH3 193, HCl 187, NH4Cl 95 J K−1 mol−1. Calculate ΔG⦵ at 298 K.

ΔH = −315 − (−46 − 95) = −174 kJ mol−1. ΔS = 95 − (193 + 187) = −285 J K−1 mol−1.
ΔG = −174 − 298(−0.285) = −174 + 84.9 = −89.1 kJ mol−1. Feasible: the white smoke of NH4Cl forms instantly when the gases meet.

Al2O3(s) + 3Mg(s) → 2Al(s) + 3MgO(s), ΔH⦵ = −130 kJ mol−1. S⦵: Al2O3 51.0, Mg 32.5, Al 28.3, MgO 27.0 J K−1 mol−1. Calculate ΔG⦵ at 298 K.

ΔS = [2(28.3) + 3(27.0)] − [51.0 + 3(32.5)] = 137.6 − 148.5 = −10.9 J K−1 mol−1.
ΔG = −130 − 298(−0.0109) = −126.8 kJ mol−1. Feasible at 298 K.

Practice: calculate ΔG⦵ at 25 °C for the combustion of ethanol, C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l). ΔHc = −1367 kJ mol−1; S⦵: C2H5OH(l) 161, O2 205, CO2 214, H2O(l) 70 J K−1 mol−1.

ΔS = [2(214) + 3(70)] − [161 + 3(205)] = 638 − 776 = −138 J K−1 mol−1.
ΔG = −1367 − 298(−0.138) = −1367 + 41 = −1326 kJ mol−1. Very negative, yet ethanol does not ignite by itself: the activation energy is high.

A reaction has ΔG⦵ = −191 kJ mol−1 at 298 K (H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl), but a mixture of the two gases kept in the dark does not react. Why?

  1. ΔG is actually positive in the dark
  2. The activation energy is high, so the rate is negligible
  3. The reaction is at equilibrium
  4. Entropy decreases

ΔG tells us the reaction is thermodynamically feasible; kinetics (activation energy) decides the rate. UV light breaks Cl–Cl bonds and the reaction then becomes explosive.

title: Temperature, spontaneity and ΔG graphs
html:
R1.4.3 The effect of temperature on spontaneity AHL

In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the −TΔS term becomes more important as temperature rises. Treat the equation as two halves and decide which one wins.

ΔHΔSΔG = ΔH − TΔSSpontaneous?Example
− (exo)+always negativeAt all temperaturesCombustion of fuels; 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2
+ (endo)−always positiveNever3O2 → 2O3 under standard conditions
− (exo)−negative at low T, positive at high TOnly below T = ΔH/ΔSHaber process; freezing of water; N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3
+ (endo)+positive at low T, negative at high TOnly above T = ΔH/ΔSThermal decomposition of CaCO3; melting ice; boiling water

The changeover temperature is where ΔG = 0, which gives:

T = ΔH ÷ ΔS    (with ΔH and ΔS in matching units)
Worked example

Find the minimum temperature at which Fe2O3(s) + 3C(s) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO(g) becomes spontaneous. ΔH⦵ = +493 kJ mol−1. S⦵ / J K−1 mol−1: Fe2O3 90.0, C 5.7, Fe 27.2, CO 198.

  1. ΔS⦵ = [2(27.2) + 3(198)] − [90.0 + 3(5.7)] = 648.4 − 107.1 = +541.3 J K−1 mol−1.
  2. Set ΔG = 0: T = 493 000 ÷ 541.3 = 911 K (638 °C).

Above 911 K, −TΔS outweighs the positive ΔH and ΔG is negative. This is why iron is extracted at high temperature. (The calculation assumes ΔH and ΔS do not change with temperature.)

Worked example

NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g), ΔH = +176 kJ mol−1. S⦵: NH4Cl 95, NH3 192, HCl 187 J K−1 mol−1. Find the minimum temperature in °C for spontaneous decomposition.

ΔS = (192 + 187) − 95 = +284 J K−1 mol−1. T = 176 000 ÷ 284 = 620 K = 347 °C.

Tungsten is extracted by WO3(s) + 3H2(g) → W(s) + 3H2O(g), ΔH⦵ = +117 kJ mol−1. S⦵: WO3 76.0, H2 65.0, W 33.0, H2O(g) 189 J K−1 mol−1 (values as given). Find the minimum temperature, in K, at which the reaction becomes feasible.

ΔS = [33.0 + 3(189)] − [76.0 + 3(65.0)] = 600 − 271 = +329 J K−1 mol−1. T = 117 000 ÷ 329 = 356 K.

Calculate the temperature, in K, above which H2(g) + ½O2(g) → H2O(g) is not feasible. ΔHf(H2O, g) = −242 kJ mol−1; S⦵: H2 131, O2 205, H2O(g) 189 J K−1 mol−1.

ΔS = 189 − [131 + ½(205)] = −44.5 J K−1 mol−1. Both ΔH and ΔS are negative, so the reaction is feasible only below T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = (−242 000) ÷ (−44.5) = 5438 K. Units are essential: forgetting to convert kJ gives 5.4 K.

Graphs of ΔG against temperature AHL

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS has the form y = mx + c, with ΔG on the y-axis and T on the x-axis:

  • y-intercept (at T = 0 K) = ΔH.
  • gradient = −ΔS (the entropy change has the opposite sign to the slope).
  • The temperature where the line crosses ΔG = 0 is the changeover temperature.

A line sloping downwards means ΔS is positive (reaction becomes more spontaneous as T rises). A line sloping upwards means ΔS is negative. Phase changes (melting, boiling) are where ΔG = 0, which is why Tb = ΔHvap ÷ ΔSvap.

Work out ΔH, ΔS and feasibility at 400 K from the graph above, then reveal

ΔH = y-intercept = −20 000 J mol−1 = −20 kJ mol−1. ΔS = −gradient = −(30 000 − (−20 000)) ÷ (600 − 0) = −50 000 ÷ 600 = −83.3 J K−1 mol−1. At 400 K the line is above zero (ΔG positive), so the reaction is not feasible; it is feasible only below about 240 K.

Using ΔH = +226 kJ mol−1 and ΔS = +162.8 J K−1 mol−1 from the lithium carbonate graph, calculate the temperature at which the decomposition just becomes feasible.

T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = 226 000 ÷ 162.8 = 1388 K (≈1390 K), where the line crosses ΔG = 0.

On a graph of ΔG against T, a reaction gives a straight line sloping downwards that crosses ΔG = 0 at 800 K. What are the signs of ΔH and ΔS?

  1. ΔH +, ΔS +
  2. ΔH +, ΔS −
  3. ΔH −, ΔS +
  4. ΔH −, ΔS −

A downward slope means −ΔS is negative, so ΔS is positive. The line starts above zero at T = 0 (positive intercept), so ΔH is positive: endothermic, spontaneous above 800 K.

title: Gibbs energy and equilibrium
html:
R1.4.4 Gibbs energy and equilibrium AHL

As a reaction proceeds, the Gibbs energy of the mixture falls until it reaches a minimum. That minimum is the equilibrium position. At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and there is no further net change. A reaction mixture always moves "downhill" in Gibbs energy towards equilibrium, from either side.

ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K     R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1    (data booklet, section 1)
ΔG⦵ln KKPosition of equilibrium
NegativePositiveK > 1Lies to the right: products favoured
Zero0K = 1Neither side favoured
PositiveNegativeK < 1Lies to the left: reactants favoured

Because K depends exponentially on ΔG⦵, a ΔG⦵ more negative than about −30 kJ mol−1 gives K so large that the reaction effectively goes to completion; more positive than +30 kJ mol−1 and it hardly happens at all.

Worked example

For 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g), ΔG⦵ = −4.7 kJ mol−1 at 298 K. Calculate K.

  1. Convert to J: ΔG⦵ = −4700 J mol−1.
  2. ln K = −ΔG⦵ ÷ RT = 4700 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 1.90.
  3. K = e1.90 = 6.7. K > 1, so products are favoured at equilibrium.
Worked example

K for a reaction is 1.0 × 10−5 at 298 K. Calculate ΔG⦵.

ΔG⦵ = −8.31 × 298 × ln(1.0 × 10−5) = −8.31 × 298 × (−11.51) = +2.85 × 104 J mol−1 = +28.5 kJ mol−1. Positive, consistent with K < 1.

Link to electrochemistry (R3.2): ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵. A positive E⦵cell gives a negative ΔG⦵, so the cell reaction is spontaneous.

Link to Le Châtelier (R2.3): for an exothermic reaction (ΔH negative), raising T makes ΔG⦵ less negative, so K decreases and equilibrium shifts left, matching what Le Châtelier's principle predicts.

ΔG⦵ for a reaction is +10.0 kJ mol−1 at 298 K. Calculate K (R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1).

ln K = −ΔG⦵ ÷ RT = −10 000 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = −4.04. K = e−4.04 = 0.0176. K < 1, so reactants are favoured, as expected for a positive ΔG⦵.

For a reaction at 298 K, K = 2.5 × 108. What can be deduced?

  1. ΔG⦵ is large and positive; reactants favoured
  2. ΔG⦵ is large and negative; the reaction goes almost to completion
  3. ΔG⦵ = 0
  4. The reaction is fast

ln K = +19.3, so ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K ≈ −48 kJ mol−1. K and ΔG⦵ say nothing about rate.

For an exothermic equilibrium, what happens to ΔG⦵ and K as the temperature is raised (assume ΔS⦵ is negative)?

  1. ΔG⦵ becomes more negative; K increases
  2. ΔG⦵ becomes less negative; K decreases
  3. ΔG⦵ is unchanged; K is unchanged
  4. ΔG⦵ becomes less negative; K increases

With ΔS negative, −TΔS is positive and grows with T, so ΔG⦵ rises and K falls: the equilibrium shifts left, just as Le Châtelier predicts for an exothermic forward reaction.

Common mistakes and exam tips AHL

  • Not converting J ↔ kJ (the biggest single source of lost marks). Write units on every line.
  • Using T in °C. Always kelvin.
  • Setting S⦵ of elements to zero (only ΔHf and ΔGf are zero for elements).
  • Forgetting coefficients when summing S⦵ values.
  • Saying a reaction with negative ΔG "happens quickly". ΔG is about direction, not rate.
  • For "explain why the reaction becomes spontaneous at high temperature": state that ΔS is positive, so −TΔS becomes more negative as T increases, until it outweighs the positive ΔH and ΔG becomes negative.
  • In ΔG = −RT ln K, use R in J (8.31) so ΔG comes out in J mol−1; convert to kJ at the end.
